chapter: Producing, state of New Orleans music
title: Is New Orleans music stronger today
summary: He says it is not strong now, describing the washed-out era and the lost spirit of early sessions.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Of your three most recent albums, is there one song that you are most happy with looking back, or do you not ever listen to your old material, always looking forward? Right. So you don't listen to the old material?
Not on, no. Not on myself, especially.
Do you think that New Orleans music is stronger today than it was, say, five years ago, and I would think you'd be, I think you're responsible for it. I'm kind of answering the question.
When you say strongly, you mean the thickness of it, or the results of it
monetarily? I guess the results and more opportunities for more local artists.

As far as I'm concerned, opportunity is always there. So, I couldn't get into that part. Whether it is as strong now as it was some years ago, and not to pinpoint five, no, it's not strong now. Now, for one thing, it is ground some through a peculiar period that wasn't heyday period. New Orleans knew exactly where it was during Fats Damanoyer. It knew where it was during the Roy Brown days. We knew where we were during early Armour Thomas, Ernie Cato. You knew exactly where that whole thing was, Jesse Hills. You could really pick them out. Barbara George, Prince Lella. And there is a particular thing, and you could play six bars, or eight bars, and you'd know. Since that time, a lot of electronics has come and gone. Computers have come in and had a big hair day and left everybody hanging somewhere strange with electronic music. So, New Orleans got caught in a big ocean of things, as strong as it is, as strong as it was, and sort of got washed out of it. So, I find that many people now, since the market is so crowded, will make a record and try and make a hit at any cost, don't care what. others, on the other hand, that played authentic New Orleans music a long time ago, will go in and do that again. So, both of those things... ... ... ... ... ... ... ...

I want others on the other hand that played authentic New Orleans music a long time ago will go in and do that again. So both of those things are, they seem like misfits to me for today. The normal growth is what that would be if it would continue growing until today. But it takes a constant flow of success for people to stand that upright and last that long. Or either be very strong to come out on the other side, which I prefer. Because whether people buy you music or not, it still should grow and not be stunted or mutated or talked about badly. So New Orleans is not as strong now. Can it be again? It will be again. Yes. Certain concepts have to die out from a small, what some people consider defeat. During an earlier day, like early mother-in-law, when guys were on the session playing and there was a solo going on, a couple of other members might get up and stand up and start snapping their fingers in second line and in the studio. It really felt like that. It was a bit more humorous. It wasn't as much business. It wasn't as much business. Of course, there wasn't much worrying about what kind of sound on the amp. It just had a general amp that played. It was a bit more humor. And it wasn't how much really. Not that how much is a bad word. that I, General Lampton played. It was a bit more human. And it wasn't how much, really. Not that how much is a bad word. But the louder you have to say how much, the softer all the other stuff can. It would take a peculiar degree of success to bring you through that. It can either come out really like a rose, like the Beatles, I think that early success is responsible for all those great songs that came out. I think without that early success, there would have been a few decent Beatles songs. But because of that success, and to live through that, to come out of that. It gives you confidence. Oh, yes. And it gives you confidence inward and outward. When you pick up the pen, you feel like you belong, and it's all right. And they've already said yes. That, as far as I'm concerned, if I was to, like I'm doing, tell someone that I believe that. I believe that works. However, for myself, I don't believe that's necessary to work. I believe whether you were getting paid or not, you are something in particular, and you do that. So I think you should write forever, play forever, whether you got paid or not. And pretty much at the same pace that you can afford.
